body:
Boiling is the surest method to kill disease-causing organisms in water, according to the CDC's guidance on making water safe in an emergency. Heat inactivates viruses, bacteria and parasites, which makes boiling a dependable option when the usual supply may be unsafe to drink.

Look at the water first. If it is cloudy, filter it before boiling. Boiling does not remove physical debris, so anything suspended in the water will still be there afterward.

Bring the water to a full rolling boil and hold it there for 1 minute. At elevations above 2,000 meters (6,500 feet), keep the rolling boil going for 3 minutes instead. Count the time from when the boil is fully rolling, not from when the water first starts to heat. These figures come from CDC emergency guidance accessed in September 2026.

Then let the water cool naturally. Once it has cooled, store it in clean, sanitized containers with tight covers so that the treated water stays protected.

Know what the method does not do. Boiling works on disease-causing organisms. It does not remove chemical toxins, heavy metals or physical debris. Water that may contain chemical contamination is not made safe by boiling alone.

review.scope: Source consistency check: verifies that factual statements (boil durations, elevation threshold, organisms inactivated, contaminants not removed, cooling and storage steps) directly reflect the provided CDC source excerpt, that attribution is accurate, and that the method's limitations are declared. Not independent laboratory or scientific verification.

sources.title: CDC — Making Water Safe in an Emergency: Boiling Water

summary: Bring water to a full rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes above 2,000 meters (6,500 feet), to kill disease-causing organisms. Boiling does not remove chemical toxins, heavy metals or physical debris.
title: Boil the water, then know what boiling misses
